govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DolanJohnF_Dola:
An FBI memorandum dated February 12, 1968 came from the Bureau's Dallas office chief. It reports that John P. Dolan had been contacted by telephone by Jim Garrison, the New Orleans district attorney then investigating President Kennedy's assassination. Dolan told the Bureau he had declined to discuss the case with Garrison.

The memo matters because the FBI tracked Garrison's moves closely while publicly standing apart from his probe. A phone call to a Dallas man became a headquarters record within the Bureau. It shows the quiet monitoring that ran alongside the most public assassination investigation of the era.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HaleyGilbertF_H:
Harold Weisberg wrote to Gilbert F. Haley on February 16, 1974 and sent more than words. He enclosed damaged copies of his Whitewash series, the books that made his name as a Warren Report critic. The letter also invites Haley into a discussion of assassination finances.

Damaged stock was a working author's problem: books that could not be sold at full price still served as evidence in the right hands. Weisberg put his into the mail with an offer to talk money and cases. The letter shows him running his one-man publishing operation, copies, costs, and all.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KennedyJohnF_Ke:
Stewart Alsop wrote in the Saturday Evening Post on April 6, 1963 about a worried president. His subject was the crisis in President Kennedy's foreign policy. Alsop called it the collapse of Kennedy's grand design, the ambitious plan with which the young president had begun.

Seven months before Dallas, a leading columnist was already writing the administration as a design in ruins. Alsop had the access and the standing to say it in America's biggest magazine. The article preserves that judgment in full, a measure of how troubled Kennedy's presidency looked from inside Washington that spring.

govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba-cub:
Adlai Stevenson, the United States ambassador to the United Nations, played a central part in ending the Cuban Missile Crisis. Peter Kornbluh edited this briefing book, number 811, published in October 2022. Its subtitle says President John F. Kennedy sacrificed his most consequential crisis adviser.

Documents chart Stevenson's work in managing and resolving the crisis. His rule was blunt: blackmail and intimidation never, negotiation and sanity always. Yet his standing at home suffered after the settlement. The posting lets readers weigh his real contribution against the political price he paid for the deal that ended the standoff.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: President John F. Kennedy worried that Israel's Dimona reactor was meant for weapons, and he pushed hard for American inspections of the site. The evidence here is the title alone, so this page serves as the short entry to that larger file on the strongest inspection demand a president ever made of Israel.
hume-history-of-england-1860-part-f:
Part F completes the 1860 Virtue edition of David Hume's History of England, closing the sixth and final part. Hume's history, published from 1754 to 1762, ends with the Glorious Revolution of 1688, where its seventy-one chapters stop. The philosopher from Edinburgh had written the book his whole century read.

The final part brings the long contest of crown and parliament to its settlement. Hume's even hand and lucid style held readers who agreed with nothing else he wrote. For a hundred years, to know English history meant to have read Hume's version of it. Part F sets the last stone on that monument, and the set stands complete.

the-evolution-of-theology-an-anthropolog: Huxley traces gods back to ghosts: how early men made spirits, then gods, then God. Bold and closely argued, it brought science to religion's roots. A landmark of free thought, a landmark of free thought.

20301-a-museum-for-young-gentlemen-and-l:
A Museum for Young Gentlemen and Ladies is a private tutor for youth at home. It gathers facts on many subjects in one small, handy book. The original was tiny, about nine centimeters in size and scope. Each line held only eight or nine words on average there.

That small scale shaped the plain, packed style of the whole work. Such books taught manners, nature, trade, and morals before school was common. A museum, then, meant a storehouse of wonders, not a building alone. Young readers got a pocket tutor full of facts worth knowing.
21047-the-nursery-no-109-january-1876-vo:
Fine drawings in this number need no praise from us, The Nursery tells its readers for January 1876. Merrill's Christmas at the North and Sheppard's at the South earn warm words. Harrison Weir's two dogs are called capital work in the same breath.

The Nursery, a monthly magazine for the youngest readers, mixes tales, verse, and plates. Large print and short pieces suit children just past picture books alone. Volume nineteen's New Year number shows its cosy store at full charm. Such magazines taught generations of American children to love the printed page, one short, bright piece at a time.
19953-origin-and-development-of-form-and:
William H. Holmes traced the origin and development of form and ornament in ceramic art. Living tribes' art, he argues, can illuminate pre-Columbian art's obscure passages. Peoples least influenced by whites preserve the oldest methods best. Holmes supplements excavation with ethnology throughout the study. Potsherds become evidence of whole design systems here. The work appeared under the Bureau of Ethnology's imprint.

Holmes was a geologist, artist, and archaeologist in one career. His ceramic studies classified decoration by its growth from technique. Basket marks, coils, and tools explain painted designs in his theory. The argument shaped American archaeology for decades. His drawings alone make the volume valuable. It is a founding text of ceramic anthropology.
20434-the-boy-scouts-first-camp-fire-or-:
The Boy Scouts' First Camp Fire, published in 1913, follows a troop of boys learning scouting with the Silver Fox patrol. Camp life, hikes, and tests of skill fill the chapters. The boys learn to watch, listen, and remember what they see.

One lesson comes straight from the instruction book. A true scout keeps his eyes and ears open to see and hear everything. The more a boy can recall from a store window after one minute's look, the higher he stands. Such drills, mixed with outdoor fun, made these books favorites with the first scouting generation.
22028-the-war-service-of-the-1-4-royal-b:
C. R. M. F. Cruttwell, a former captain in the battalion, wrote The War Service of the 1/4 Royal Berkshire Regiment at his old commanding officer's request. The history first ran in the Berkshire Chronicle in 1920, while the Great War was still fresh. Berkshire families then paid to see it reprinted as a book. Cruttwell follows a Territorial battalion of county men through the whole war.

Such regimental histories record marches, trenches, attacks, and the names of the fallen. This one was made for the men who served and the homes that lost them. Its value now lies in the detail only an insider could supply. It shows how one English county battalion endured the First World War.
